sessionStart.prompt: Route these task categories through the matching flow-* skill: an .arc42 chapter, an architecture decision record, a technical debt record, or an architecture proposal -> flow-arc42; the domain model in .domain -> flow-domain; the technology graph in .tech -> flow-tech; design guidelines in .design -> flow-design; the AI adoption record in .ai -> flow-ai (each of those five stops and says so when the repository has not adopted the folder, and each loads the repository's own instruction files for the folder rather than carrying rules of its own); feature work -> flow-feature; bug fixes -> flow-bug; existing repository structure or layout refactors, folder moves, project/solution organization fixes, or test/harness placement changes -> flow-structure; new module or service -> flow-create-module, flow-create-service; dependency or package updates -> flow-update-packages; Aspire upgrades -> flow-aspire-update; MVP creation -> flow-create-mvp; repository or project scaffolding -> flow-repo, flow-project; any other task category no flow-* skill covers, such as tooling, CI, scripting, or housekeeping -> flow-fallback. This list is the plugin-provided baseline, not an exhaustive catalog: a repository may provide additional repo-native flow-* skills in the host's own skill folder, and those take precedence for the task categories they cover. flow-fallback is the last resort, not an escape hatch: use it only when no skill covers the category or when the matched skill targets fundamentally different work, never because a matching skill's preconditions are unmet. If you decide not to use a flow skill for one of these categories, say so explicitly and give the reason before continuing. A flow is one session: fan-out across sessions and worktrees belongs to the fleet plugin, never to a flow. Every flow reports progress through whichever delivery surface is bound, resolved by pattern from the live tool list rather than by a hardcoded tool prefix, and no surface bound is a normal outcome that never blocks a stage. A repository declares its bindings, extensions, policy, and gates in .devbook/config.json; configuration chooses among behaviour the engine already implements and never adds a stage. Configuration may add human gates anywhere; it may never remove the Personal Validation gate or hand a gate to a plugin. Model choice is personal and never comes from the repository: it is resolved from the model-override host slot, and .devbook/config.json carries no model key. A repository declares how its application starts, and where, in its own start skill at .agents/skills/start.md, and its QA depth in policy; nothing to start is extensions.app.start set to null. The repository's own MCP configuration and instruction files remain the source of truth for MCP servers.
